Tier 1 adds lightweight on-device embedding models like MiniLM or EmbeddingGemma to unlock semantic features.

Tier 3 brings in prose LLMs (BYOK or hosted) to generate rewrites, bridges, examples, while Jev verifies meaning preservation and register fit — a generate-then-verify cascade. Tier 4 extends to media models: image generation for scene sketches, music/ambient for mood, TTS voices for dialogue casting.

These tools are explicit-only, never automatic, framed purely as writing aids: if a generated image misses a detail you cared about, your prose didn't convey it — the image acts as a mirror of your text, not decoration, and the same logic applies to narrated audio, mood-matched music scored against the scene's tone, and animatics that test whether blocking reads clearly. The core reframe is treating media models as readers reporting back what your text actually communicates.

This opens a neat loop: render an image, caption it with a vision-language model, then have the text model compare that caption against the passage's intended details — flagging "the image lost: the red coat, the rain" — which surfaces exactly which sentence-level details survived translation and highlights under-specified spans. On the embeddings-for-grammar question, I'm thinking about what contextual word-choice checks a small masked-language model could enable, like a fill-mask pipeline for catching awkward phrasing.

Sentence embeddings could also flag redundant sentences, detect orphan sentences that don't fit their paragraph's centroid (suggesting repositioning — the user's exact idea, done locally), cluster revision attempts to surface the most distinct ones, and with multilingual embedding models like XLM-R extend word-alternative suggestions beyond English since Harper only covers that language. For span selection, I'm thinking sentence IDs (S01, S02...) with choices capped under 255 options.

For connecting sentences, I'm picturing a workflow: select a sentence, surface top candidate partners via embeddings, then classify the relation type per pair (supports, contradicts, repeats, sets up, pays off, unrelated), checking whether a reader would actually need that link made explicit. These render as threads in the margin, with manual connection possible (select A, "Connect to...", click B), auto-labeled relation, optional LLM-generated bridge text, and the link persisting as a discussable thread with personas. For positioning, I'm working out how to generate candidate slots for where a selected sentence could move.

Then for Sentence Lab, I'm rethinking capture: attempts should only register as complete sentences (terminal punctuation or a pause threshold), near-duplicates should be deduped by edit distance, and rewrite counts should reflect distinct completed versions rather than every keystroke pause. Each full-sentence rewrite would then be labeled with a specific move — Shorter, Plainer, Concrete, Active, Reordered, Stronger verb, Rhythm — to make the pattern of revision visible.

I'm also sketching features around this: a one-line delta summary for each rewrite, inline diff previews in the manuscript itself, a clickable word strip offering ranked alternatives with register labels, a lineage timeline letting the user splice phrases from different attempts together, and a "try it elsewhere" option for repositioning sentences.

For evaluation, each candidate gets scored on meaning preservation, register fit, and clarity, with failing candidates flagged or hidden and sorting left under user control. And rather than relying on a model for generation, I want deterministic transforms doing the actual rewriting — trimming hedges and filler words, splitting at conjunctions, front-loading main clauses, converting nominalizations, and switching passive to active voice only when the agent is stated.

For proactivity, the principle is "compute ahead, reveal on attention": a background pipeline precomputes grammar checks and alternates for the cursor paragraph during pauses, surfacing them as subtle indicators like small glyphs next to a sentence ("3 rewrites ready") that cost nothing to ignore. Cards only interrupt when a threshold for helpfulness is crossed and the writer isn't in flow, while hovering or selecting reveals the precomputed results instantly with no loading delay.

I'm also thinking about Jev-driven highlight "lenses" — toggles that paint the document to show claims, abstract passages, slow sentences, or what a skimmer would notice, scoring each sentence and rendering it as a heat underline. Writers could even define their own lens by typing a question like "where do I sound defensive?" and having Jev score each sentence against it, essentially giving them semantic search over their own draft, capped at 255 sentences per request.

Then there's the image generation idea: selecting a descriptive passage and feeding it to an image model to visualize the scene.

Extending that, the rendered image could get a caption from a vision-language model, and Jev would check each concrete detail sentence against that caption to flag what the picture lost or misrepresented — like missing the window or the cold. There's also room for mood boards and character reference sheets in the dossier, with Jev comparing later descriptions against the sheet for continuity, catching things like eye color changing between chapters.

For audio, beyond the existing local TTS and speech follow-along, I'm considering reading selections aloud, A/B comparing rewrites by ear, casting different voices per character with Jev attributing dialogue lines automatically, and judging rhythm by listening rather than reading.

For music, generating a short ambient bed matching a scene's tone could help with immersion and flagging tonal inconsistency across chapters, though I should be honest that this is atmosphere rather than real critique — the actual useful critique is scoring tension/warmth/pace per section and tracking that curve, with the music being a playful rendering on top. Video animatics for action sequences could test staging clarity but are expensive and low priority. Voice design for TTS from character descriptions could help verify that characters actually sound distinct from each other.

Now I'm sketching the roadmap: Phase 1 fixes core capture/rewrite/word-alternative tools with inline preview and Jev ranking, plus selection palette additions (Rephrase/Words/Move/Hear). Phase 2 builds a local sentence-embeddings index replacing TF-IDF for positioning, semantic echo, orphan sentences, and idea repetition. Phase 3 adds thread-spanning connections, role spine, and dialogue attribution. Phase 4 covers media instruments like captioned "picture it," voice casting, and mood generation — and I should merge the old "You wrote" echo card into the new semantic threads feature.

I'm cataloging concrete problems with the current system: the struggle-tracker commits whatever's on screen at a 1.2s pause, so half-deleted fragments get logged as "earlier tries" and inflate rewrite counts; without a prose provider, Sentence Lab just shows the user's own fragments with a "connect a model" notice; variants are unlabeled with no diff or in-text preview and only replace whole sentences; Harper sits in its own panel disconnected from Sentence Lab; and since transformers.js is already shipped for TTS, adding embeddings or fill-mask is a small lift. I'm also noting a local MiniCPM option for desktop.

I'm flagging more gaps: no equivalent local provider exists for web, the "jev" gate only answers whether to show a suggestion rather than what to suggest, and the selection menu is limited to just three actions. I want to verify the pause-to-commit timing in the code — tracing the 400ms setTimeout that triggers evaluation and the commitVersion call to confirm exactly when a fragment gets locked in as a prior attempt.

input.content:
# From cards to instruments

Design proposal, 2026-10-09. Responds to `audit.md` (2026-10-05) and its proposed cards. Nothing here is implemented yet.

## The problem in one paragraph

Twyne's help is shaped like notifications. Local rules decide that something might be worth saying, Jev decides whether to say it, and a card describes it in the margin. Most cards *describe* ("You wrote", "Possible repetition", "Say it plainly first") instead of *doing* something to the text. Without a prose model the tools have almost nothing to offer: they show the writer's own fragments back to them and suggest connecting a model. Jev, the cheapest and fastest model available, is used mostly as a yes/no gate in front of cards. It is rarely used to point at spans, choose a position, or rank candidates, which is what it does best.

## Why Sentence Lab feels broken (verified in code)

1. **The "earlier tries" are mid-edit snapshots, not attempts.** `struggle-tracker.ts:85` commits a version after every 1.2 s pause, and `commitVersion` (`struggle-signals.ts`) stores the previous wording whenever exactly one sentence changed. A pause in the middle of a word records something like `The river carr the town's memory.` as an attempt.
2. **Sentence identity depends on position.** When the paragraph's sentence count changes, `commitVersion` clears `rewrites` and `attempts`. Splitting, joining, or moving a sentence erases its history. Activity is keyed by block position, so moving a sentence elsewhere is not visible at all.
3. **Without a prose provider there is nothing to show.** `fillSpec` (`in-flow-tools.ts`) returns the seed and the notice "Your own attempts only — connect a model in Settings for fresh variants." The tool's main content then comes from item 1.
4. **The variants carry no reasons.** The prompt asks for three different approaches (reorder, cut, make concrete), but the UI labels them all "Other ways". Nothing checks whether a variant keeps the meaning.
5. **The tool covers only wording.** It has no word-level alternatives, no placement, no read-aloud, and no comparison in context.

## Critique of the proposed cards in `audit.md`

| Proposal | Keep | Problem | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Three ways forward | The core idea: complete alternatives you can choose, edit, compare, or keep original | The generator labels its own variants ("Shorter"); it needs a prose model; it is still a card | Code computes facts like word count and voice; Jev or embeddings check meaning; rule-based rewrites and on-device models fill it offline |
| Find the exact word | Yes | Assumes an LLM | Works offline: thesaurus candidates ranked by a small masked language model in context; Jev adds nuance tags |
| Evidence with limits | Yes, later | Large dependency on fetching sources | Leave in research; reuse the claim span from the Threads index |
| Show the shape | Yes | "Constrained schema" still lets a model invent nodes | Every node must be a span of the writer's text. Jev picks spans and edge types; code draws |
| One concrete example | Partly | Invented examples are a hallucination risk in nonfiction | Offer only sourced examples, the writer's own notebook scraps, or examples clearly labelled hypothetical |
| Bridge these two thoughts | Yes | No trigger defined | A drop in embedding similarity between neighbours is the trigger; Jev names the relation; the LLM drafts a transition |
| Recover the useful attempt | Yes | Depends on attempt history, which is currently corrupted (see above) | Fix capture first |
| A next step you choose | No | Still general coaching | Replace with **Say it**: the writer speaks what they mean and the transcript becomes a candidate sentence |

Gaps shared by every proposal:

- **They remain cards.** None of them changes where help appears. Everything still lives in a margin column, away from the words it concerns.
- **They don't cover the offline case.** Every useful proposal assumes a prose LLM, and that is the main complaint.
- **They use Jev only as a gate.** Jev can choose among up to 255 IDs in one question (the TypeSafe "line-by-line search" cookbook pattern). With sentence IDs as the options, Jev can point to *where*: which sentence this depends on, where this sentence fits, and which earlier line it repeats. None of the proposals use this.
- **They ignore other modalities.** Listening to prose read aloud is the oldest revision technique there is, and Twyne already includes a local TTS model.
- **They don't fix the foundation.** Positional identity, polluted attempts, fragile 14-word regex anchors, and the Convex-client gate in front of the writer's own judgement endpoint (`struggle-tracker.ts` `ask`: `if (!client) throw new Error("offline")`) would also undermine every new card.

What the audit gets right and should be kept: label each suggestion's provenance (rule, judgement model, text model, external lookup), give the writer control over when things appear, and measure applied edits instead of card opens.

## The reframe: three places help can live

Replace "cards" with **instruments**: tools that point at a span and change it, always with a preview and undo.

1. **In the line.** Underlines, ghost text, and small glyphs placed directly in the manuscript, like Grammarly but for a literary writer. Examples: grammar (Harper, already shipped), word alternatives, words a model finds unlikely in context, repetition. All of these run locally.
2. **Between lines (threads).** Typed links between spans: *repeats, sets up, pays off, supports, contradicts, answers, refers back to*. They appear when the writer selects or hovers with a modifier key, or when a "Threads" lens is turned on. The curve-drawing code in `flow-surface.tsx` already draws card-to-passage links; extend it to draw sentence-to-sentence links with labels.
3. **On the bench.** A focused workbench opened on one span: the Sentence bench, the Paragraph bench, and the Scene bench (described below).

**Surfacing rule.** Nothing appears automatically unless it carries a change ready to apply or opens a working instrument with one click. Pure information ("You wrote this earlier") is not allowed. The current echo card either becomes **Recover**, which offers a concrete merge, or a **thread**, which names the relationship.

## The capability ladder: what works without model access

Every instrument declares what it can do at each tier. The lowest tier must still be useful by itself. "Connect a model" is never the main content.

| Tier | What it is | Status in Twyne |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0. Code | Harper grammar and spelling; rule-based transforms; the writer's own *settled* attempts; a bundled thesaurus; TF-IDF | Harper and TF-IDF are shipped |
| 1. On-device models (opt-in download) | transformers.js: sentence embeddings, a fill-mask model (word alternatives and surprise), Whisper (Say it); Supertonic TTS (Hear it); MiniCPM5-2B on desktop (full rewrites); browser built-in rewriter or proofreader APIs where the browser provides them (feature-detected) | `@huggingface/transformers` is already a dependency; Supertonic and the desktop LiteRT provider are shipped; the download-manifest pattern exists in `browser-inference.ts` |
| 2. Jev | Selects, ranks, labels, and verifies. Generates no text, so it can afford to run on every candidate set | Shipped, but used mainly as a gate |
| 3. Prose LLM | Rewrites, bridges, merges, examples | Shipped, but its absence leaves tools empty |
| 4. Media models | Image, music, video. Always explicit, never automatic; each use shows its cost and where the data goes | Not present |

**Generators propose; Jev decides.** Candidates come from rules, the masked model, an LLM, the writer's past attempts, and the writer's speech. Jev, or local embeddings as a fallback, judges them. Anything code can compute stays in code: word count, voice, sentence-initial verb, removed hedges. Jev is asked only for meaning, register, and fit.

## Instrument 1: the Sentence bench (replaces Sentence Lab)

Fix the data first:

- **Settled attempts only.** Record a wording only when the sentence is complete (ends in terminal punctuation), the cursor has left it or about 5 s have passed, Harper reports no spelling error touching the edited span (this catches `carr`), and it is not a prefix of a later wording. Collapse near-duplicates (fewer than 3 characters different).
- **A sentence ledger.** Give each sentence a stable ID that is mapped through transactions. Re-match by fuzzy similarity rather than index, so split, join, cut, and paste preserve history. Detect moves: text deleted and reinserted at least 90% similar, either in one transaction or by cut and then paste. Each entry keeps `wordings[]` and `placements[]`.

The bench has five sections. Every candidate is a complete sentence shown as a word-level diff against the current one. Hovering a candidate previews it as ghost text in place, between the real neighbouring sentences.

1. **Rewrite.** Three to five complete alternatives. Each shows facts computed in code (`−6 words`, `active`, `no hedge`) and verified tags (`keeps meaning 0.94`, `fits your register`), plus a provenance chip: *yours (4 min ago)*, *rule*, *on-device*, *Claude*, *spoken*. Offline sources are the best settled attempt plus rule transforms (front a trailing clause, cut intensifiers and hedges, turn a nominalisation back into a verb, split at a semicolon or conjunction, join with the next sentence), each checked by Harper. On desktop, MiniCPM fills in automatically.
2. **Words.** Click any word to see alternatives in context. Thesaurus candidates are ranked by the masked model's probability in the actual sentence. Jev adds nuance (`stronger`, `plainer`, `more formal`) and a `changes meaning` warning. Repeated words in the paragraph are underlined.
3. **Place.** Insertion carets in the manuscript mark the strongest slots, each with a reason. Some reasons are deterministic: a sentence starting with *This*, *These*, *It*, or *Such* needs its antecedent before it. Others come from embedding coherence with the neighbours on each side, or from a Jev Choice over slot IDs. Uses `placements[]`: "You've tried this in 3 places; read each one in context." One click moves it, with undo.
4. **Hear.** Supertonic reads the previous sentence followed by each candidate, entirely offline. Rhythm problems are easier to hear than to see.
5. **Say it.** The writer records themselves explaining what the sentence should say. Whisper transcribes it; rules or a model tidy it; the result becomes a candidate. This replaces the "Say it plainly first" template with an actual action.

The bench opens from a struggle signal (three *settled* rewrites), after a sentence has moved twice (opens on Place), or on request from the selection menu or a shortcut.

## Instrument 2: the contextual selection menu

Today the menu always offers the same three actions (Get sources, Add margin, Send to persona). Instead, classify the selection: its **shape** locally (word, phrase, sentence, several sentences, paragraph, two separate ranges) and its **kind** with one cached Jev Choice (claim, description, dialogue, transition, list, quotation). Then offer actions to match:

| Selection | Actions |
| --- | --- |
| A word | Alternatives in the line, every use in the draft |
| A sentence | Rewrite, Move, Hear, Threads |
| A claim | Find support, How strongly to state it, Strongest objection |
| Description | See it, What's missing, Hear it |
| Dialogue | Cast voices, Does each speaker sound distinct? |
| Two ranges (Alt+select) | Name the relation, Bridge, Merge, Which is stronger, Swap |

The existing three actions remain.

## Instrument 3: Threads

- Number the sentences of the current section (`S001`…). Jev Choice accepts at most 255 options, and state plus the longest question must fit in 32k tokens, so use section windows plus a second pass (the cookbook's two-pass approach).

## The problem in one paragraph

Twyne's help is shaped like notifications. Local rules decide that something might be worth saying, Jev decides whether to say it, and a card describes it in the margin. Most cards *describe* ("You wrote", "Possible repetition", "Say it plainly first") instead of *doing* something to the text. Without a prose model the tools have almost nothing to offer: they show the writer's own fragments back to them and suggest connecting a model. Jev, the cheapest and fastest model available, is used mostly as a yes/no gate in front of cards. It is rarely used to point at spans, choose a position, or rank candidates, which is what it does best.

## Why Sentence Lab feels broken (verified in code)

1. **The "earlier tries" are mid-edit snapshots, not attempts.** `struggle-tracker.ts:85` commits a version after every 1.2 s pause, and `commitVersion` (`struggle-signals.ts`) stores the previous wording whenever exactly one sentence changed. A pause in the middle of a word records something like `The river carr the town's memory.` as an attempt.
2. **Sentence identity depends on position.** When the paragraph's sentence count changes, `commitVersion` clears `rewrites` and `attempts`. Splitting, joining, or moving a sentence erases its history. Activity is keyed by block position, so moving a sentence elsewhere is not visible at all.
3. **Without a prose provider there is nothing to show.** `fillSpec` (`in-flow-tools.ts`) returns the seed and the notice "Your own attempts only — connect a model in Settings for fresh variants." The tool's main content then comes from item 1.
4. **The variants carry no reasons.** The prompt asks for three different approaches (reorder, cut, make concrete), but the UI labels them all "Other ways". Nothing checks whether a variant keeps the meaning.
5. **The tool covers only wording.** It has no word-level alternatives, no placement, no read-aloud, and no comparison in context.

| Proposal | Keep | Problem | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Three ways forward | The core idea: complete alternatives you can choose, edit, compare, or keep original | The generator labels its own variants ("Shorter"); it needs a prose model; it is still a card | Code computes facts like word count and voice; Jev or embeddings check meaning; rule-based rewrites and on-device models fill it offline |
| Find the exact word | Yes | Assumes an LLM | Works offline: thesaurus candidates ranked by a small masked language model in context; Jev adds nuance tags |
| Evidence with limits | Yes, later | Large dependency on fetching sources | Leave in research; reuse the claim span from the Threads index |
| Show the shape | Yes | "Constrained schema" still lets a model invent nodes | Every node must be a span of the writer's text. Jev picks spans and edge types; code draws |
| One concrete example | Partly | Invented examples are a hallucination risk in nonfiction | Offer only sourced examples, the writer's own notebook scraps, or examples clearly labelled hypothetical |
| Bridge these two thoughts | Yes | No trigger defined | A drop in embedding similarity between neighbours is the trigger; Jev names the relation; the LLM drafts a transition |
| Recover the useful attempt | Yes | Depends on attempt history, which is currently corrupted (see above) | Fix capture first |
| A next step you choose | No | Still general coaching | Replace with **Say it**: the writer speaks what they mean and the transcript becomes a candidate sentence |

- **They remain cards.** None of them changes where help appears. Everything still lives in a margin column, away from the words it concerns.
- **They don't cover the offline case.** Every useful proposal assumes a prose LLM, and that is the main complaint.
- **They use Jev only as a gate.** Jev can choose among up to 255 IDs in one question (the TypeSafe "line-by-line search" cookbook pattern). Some reasons are deterministic: a sentence starting with *This*, *These*, *It*, or *Such* needs its antecedent before it. Others come from embedding coherence with the neighbours on each side, or from a Jev Choice over slot IDs. Uses `placements[]`: "You've tried this in 3 places; read each one in context." One click moves it, with undo.
4. **Hear.** Supertonic reads the previous sentence followed by each candidate, entirely offline. Rhythm problems are easier to hear than to see.
5. **Say it.** The writer records themselves explaining what the sentence should say. Whisper transcribes it; rules or a model tidy it; the result becomes a candidate. This replaces the "Say it plainly first" template with an actual action.

The bench opens from a struggle signal (three *settled* rewrites), after a sentence has moved twice (opens on Place), or on request from the selection menu or a shortcut.

## Instrument 2: the contextual selection menu

Today the menu always offers the same three actions (Get sources, Add margin, Send to persona). Instead, classify the selection: its **shape** locally (word, phrase, sentence, several sentences, paragraph, two separate ranges) and its **kind** with one cached Jev Choice (claim, description, dialogue, transition, list, quotation). Then offer actions to match:

| Selection | Actions |
| --- | --- |
| A word | Alternatives in the line, every use in the draft |
| A sentence | Rewrite, Move, Hear, Threads |
| A claim | Find support, How strongly to state it, Strongest objection |
| Description | See it, What's missing, Hear it |
| Dialogue | Cast voices, Does each speaker sound distinct? |
| Two ranges (Alt+select) | Name the relation, Bridge, Merge, Which is stronger, Swap |

The existing three actions remain.

## Instrument 3: Threads

- Number the sentences of the current section (`S001`…). Jev Choice accepts at most 255 options, and state plus the longest question must fit in 32k tokens, so use section windows plus a second pass (the cookbook's two-pass approach).
- Local embeddings propose candidate pairs at no cost. One Jev request labels them: a Choice among *repeats / supports / contradicts / sets up / pays off / answers / no real relation*, plus a Noul for whether the link exists (Choice probabilities always sum to 1).
- Proactive threads that come with an action: a **setup with no payoff** ("'the ledger' is introduced in ¶2 and never comes back": choose a later sentence or add one); **two sentences doing the same job** (offer Merge with an actual merged sentence, or keep the stronger, chosen by Jev); a **dangling reference** (*this* with nothing before it to refer to: offer Move).
- Replace the 14-word regex anchors with ProseMirror decorations keyed to ledger IDs.

## Instrument 4: the Scene bench (where media models earn their place)

Images, music, and video help a writer only if they show the gap between what is on the page and what the writer imagines.

- **See it.** Jev runs a Noul for each scene dimension (place, time of day, light, weather, who is present, what they wear, spatial layout, sound, smell). The image prompt is built **only from spans of the writer's text**, which Jev selects rather than writes. The result is the image plus a list of **what it had to invent**. Each invented item links to the spot where the writer could specify it. That list is the useful output; the image is the hook.
- **Continuity** without images: extract attributes as text ("Mara's coat: red, ch. 2"; "blue, ch. 7") and flag contradictions as threads across folios.
- **Voices.** Assign TTS voices to speakers and play the dialogue back. If two characters sound the same aloud, they also read the same.
- **Tension curve.** Jev Scores per paragraph (tension, pace, warmth) plotted across a chapter cost almost nothing and show pacing. An optional generated music cue turns the curve into sound, a quick way to check whether a scene feels as tense as intended.
- **Blocking.** Positions and movements chosen from spans become a simple top-down SVG. Generated video ("animate the beat") stays a late opt-in for screenwriters; the diagram does more for the writing at a tiny fraction of the cost.

## Local language models as grammar and style checks

- **Surprise underline.** A masked model scores each word in context. Unlikely words catch real-word errors that Harper misses (*form/from*, wrong prepositions, malapropisms), and the model's top replacements become suggestions.
- **Redundancy.** Neighbouring sentences with very similar embeddings.
- **Cohesion gaps.** Similarity between neighbours falls below this draft's own baseline; this is the trigger for Bridge.
- **Voice match.** Distance from the centroid of the writer's voice samples in the notebook. Phrase it as an observation, never a verdict.
- **Clichés.** Phrase embeddings compared against a small bundled list.
- **Drift from the dossier.** Similarity to the stated goal, continuous across the draft, with Jev confirming only at the peaks.

## Jev question shapes (concrete)

| Need | Primitive | State | Options |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Where should S go? | Choice | Section with `S###` IDs and `slot###` markers | slot IDs + `nowhere better` |
| What does S depend on? | Choice + Noul exists | Section with IDs | sentence IDs |
| Relation between A and B | Choice | Both spans + surrounding text | the 7 relation types |
| Does candidate keep meaning? | Noul (one per candidate) | Original, candidate, paragraph | — |
| Register fit | Score | Candidate + dossier tone + voice sample | 3 levels |
| Which word fits | Choice | Sentence with the word slot marked | candidates + `keep original` |
| Is scene dimension X specified? | Noul (one per dimension) | Passage | — |
| Which spans are visual detail? | Choice over span IDs (repeated with exclusions) or one Noul per span | Passage with span IDs | span IDs |

Batch every independent question for the same state into one request (`system-one.ts` already supports this).

## Foundation fixes (prerequisites)

1. Settled attempts and the sentence ledger (above).
2. Let callers use a custom judgement endpoint without a Convex client (audit gap 8; also `struggle-tracker.ts` `ask`).
3. Mark candidates as `asked` only after the judgement succeeds; re-index the archive when earlier paragraphs change (audit gaps 5 and 6).
4. Remove the "You wrote" echo, or turn it into Recover or a thread.
5. Measure applied edits, edits still kept after 24 h, time until typing resumes after an instrument closes, and the reason for each dismissal. Do not measure opens.

## Phasing

1. **Offline Sentence bench**: settled attempts, sentence ledger, rule rewrites validated by Harper, thesaurus word alternatives, Hear with Supertonic, ghost preview, inline diff, MiniCPM on desktop. Useful with no network at all.
2. **Jev as selector**: Place, Threads, meaning and register checks on candidates, the contextual selection menu.
3. **On-device model bundle** (opt-in download): embeddings, fill-mask surprise and ranking, Whisper for Say it; replaces TF-IDF echoes.
4. **Scene bench**: See it with the invented-details list, the continuity ledger, voices, and the tension curve; image and music providers behind explicit consent.

content.text:
I wrote the full proposal to `docs/writing-instruments.md`. No app code has changed yet. The scores in the mockup are illustrative.

## Why Sentence Lab shows you fragments

I traced it in the code. There are three separate causes:

- **The "earlier tries" are snapshots taken mid-edit.** The tracker saves a version after every 1.2-second pause (`struggle-tracker.ts:85`). It then stores whatever the sentence looked like before as an "attempt". If you stop to think halfway through a word, something like `The river carr the town's memory.` is saved as one of your tries.
- **A sentence is tracked only by its position.** Splitting, joining or moving sentences wipes the paragraph's rewrite history (`commitVersion` in `struggle-signals.ts`). Moving a sentence around, which you said you do, can't be seen at all.
- **With no model connected, those fragments are all it has.** Without a prose model, the tool shows only those snapshots plus a note telling you to connect a model.

So the fix starts with how attempts are captured. A wording should only count once the sentence is finished and you've left it. Each sentence also needs a stable ID that survives being moved.

## Critique of the Codex proposals

They're good ideas with the same four gaps:

1. **They're all still cards.** Nothing changes where help appears.
2. **Every useful one needs a prose model.** That leaves the offline case, which is your main complaint, unsolved.
3. **They use Jev only as a yes/no gate.** Jev can choose among up to 255 IDs in one question. Give each sentence an ID and Jev can point at things: where a moved sentence fits best, which earlier line it repeats, what a "this" refers back to. That's what makes placement and span connections practical.
4. **They don't fix the broken plumbing above.** Any new card would be built on the same bad attempt history.

"A next step you choose" is the weakest proposal. In its place I'd add **Say it**: you speak what you mean, it's transcribed, and the transcript becomes one of the candidate sentences.

## Where the other model types fit

- **Small models running in the app (embedding and word-prediction models)** do the most for the least. They can rank alternative words by how well they fit the actual sentence, which is the Grammarly-style feature, offline. They can flag correctly spelled wrong words like "form/from" that the grammar checker misses. They can also spot two sentences doing the same job, and gaps between paragraphs that need a bridge. The library for this (`@huggingface/transformers`) is already installed.
- **Voice** is the cheapest win, because the local text-to-speech is already shipped. Hearing each alternative read after the sentence before it shows rhythm problems quickly.
- **Image generation** helps the writing only if it shows the gap between the page and your intent. Jev checks what the passage actually specifies (time of day, light, who is present). The image prompt is built only from your own words. The useful output is the list of things the image had to invent, each linked to the spot where you could add it.
- **Music** works best as a mirror of mood. A tension curve across a chapter, from Jev scores, is the real tool; a generated cue is optional.
- **Video** should come last. A simple top-down diagram of who stands where does more for a scene than an animated clip.

## Suggested next step

Phase 1 of the doc is a Sentence bench that works with no network at all:
- attempts saved only once a sentence is finished, and sentence IDs that survive moves;
- complete rewrites from simple rules, checked by the existing grammar checker (Harper);
- word alternatives from a bundled thesaurus;
- "Hear" using the local voice;
- in-place previews with a word-by-word diff.

On desktop, the bundled local model can fill in fuller rewrites. Phase 2 adds the Jev-driven placement, span connections, and a selection menu that changes with what you select.

Should I start on Phase 1?

content.content:
## What `<rich-input>` Is

`<rich-input>` (by Bram.us, on GitHub and npm) is a Web Component that behaves like a normal single-line text input. It adds keyword-based autocompletion and syntax highlighting inside the field. The page calls it "search engine-grade filter intelligence" for ordinary web forms. Users can type plain free text, structured `keyword:value` filters (e.g., `label:"We Play House Recordings"`, `year:2026`), or both.

**Scope note:** The page does not mention chips, @-mentions, or embedded inline widgets. All "rich" behavior is text highlighting within the input plus a suggestion popover.

## Fields, Tokens, and Inline Elements

- **Keywords:** Each comes from a nested `<datalist>`. Its `id` becomes the keyword (case-insensitive), `label` sets the display name, and `data-type="number"` marks numeric fields. The demos use label, year, artist, style, and playlist.
- **Values:** These come from `<option>` elements. Values containing spaces are quoted automatically. Options can include custom HTML such as logos or avatars, but only the plain value is inserted.
- **Operators:** Prefixes such as `-`, `~`, `+` (e.g., `-style:Acid`). The default is `['-']`.
- **Combinators:** Logical words such as AND, OR, NOT, XOR. There are none by default.
- **Delimiters:** Grouping pairs such as `()`, `[]`, `{}`. The default is `['()']`.
- **Invalid tokens:** Unknown keywords, or values not in the datalist, get a wavy underline.

Each token type has its own highlight name: `rich-input-keyword`, `-operator`, `-combinator`, `-delimiter`, `-invalid`, plus one per keyword (e.g., `::highlight(label)`).

## How Interactions Work

- **Typing triggers:** Autocomplete works at two levels. Typing `a` offers `artist:`, and typing `label:"K` offers Keinemusik and Kranky. Combinators are also suggested.
- **Popover position:** The popover is pinned to the start of the current token (e.g., its opening quote) rather than following the caret.
- **Clear button:** Appears once the field has text.
- **Events:**
  - `rich-input-select` fires when a suggestion is chosen.
  - `search` fires when Enter is pressed with no suggestions open.

## Technical Approach

- **Native Web Component** with no configuration needed beyond the markup.
- **OpaqueRange API (Chromium 152+):**
  - `input.createValueRange(start, end)` creates ranges for highlighting.
  - `getBoundingClientRect()` positions the popover.
  - `range.disconnect()` cleans up ranges after edits.
- **CSS Custom Highlight API:** Styles text inside the native input without overlay divs.
- **Fallback for Safari 17.2+ and Firefox 141+:** A `[contenteditable]` element in the shadow DOM handles highlighting, and a hidden mirror div positions the popover. Page-level `::highlight()` rules are copied into the shadow stylesheet automatically. A child `<style>` block can also be injected.
- **Form association:** Uses `formAssociated = true` and ElementInternals, so it works with form submission, FormData, and reset.
- **Dynamic datalists:** A MutationObserver picks up datalists added or changed at runtime.
- **Styling hooks:** Shadow parts include input, control, icon, clear-button, popover, suggestions-header, suggestions-list, suggestion-item (plus -active and -selected), suggestion-content, and suggestion-image.
- **JavaScript API:**
  - `value`
  - `operators`, `combinators`, `delimiters` (per instance or as static defaults)
  - `getParsedQuery()`, which returns `{ raw, tokens }`
  - `getKeywords()`
  - `focus()`, `blur()`, `select()`, `setSelectionRange()`

## Examples

**Live demo presets:**
- Quoted music search
- House subgenre
- Artist & style
- Free text plus keywords
- Invalid value
- Negative filter
- OR combinator
- Grouped query with delimiters

**Numbered examples:**
1. **Parsed Query Inspector:** Shows the detected tokens and `getParsedQuery()` output live.
2. **Form Integration:** Demonstrates submit and reset.
3. **Shadow Parts Theming:** A pill theme and a retro terminal theme.
4. **Rich Option & Image Styling:** Logos shown as circular avatars.
5. **Custom Leading Icon:** One version uses an emoji via `content`, another an SVG via `background`.
6. **Dynamic Datalists:** A button adds a "bpm" filter to every instance on the page.
7. **Operators, Combinators & Delimiters:** An interactive configurator with presets (grouped, prefix operators, custom syntax), live HTML/JS code, and parsed query parts.

The key realization is that rich-input essentially does syntax highlighting for a formal keyword:value grammar, so I want to extend that idea generally and specifically to Twyne.

content.thinking:
I'm thinking about `<rich-input>` as a single-line web component that highlights `keyword:value` tokens via the CSS Custom Highlight API, with autocomplete and a parsed-query output—so plain text gets recognized in place and turned into structure while remaining plain text. Pairing this with System One, I see the deterministic grammar handling explicit syntax like `year:2026` while Jev handles natural language into that same token structure.

Jev could produce "soft tokens" recognized from free prose without explicit syntax, like spotting "nurses" as the audience and "already know triage" as their existing knowledge. I'm also considering how this would scale across Twyne's many fields—dossier fields, comment composer, search, persona prompts, bibliography, rubric criteria, slash commands, saved tool configs—and how the existing field-level Jev Score grading (Vague/Partial/Specific/Sharp) could become span-level highlighting instead, showing which words carry weight versus decoration as you type, using a span-ID pattern where candidate spans are pre-segmented in code and Jev judges over those span IDs.

I'm working through the technical mechanism: the CSS Custom Highlight API can style text inside native inputs without altering the DOM, though it's unclear how it handles text nodes inside native `<input>` elements versus textareas, with contenteditable as a fallback for Safari/Firefox. I don't need to dig deeper into that mechanism right now—I should move on to brainstorming a concrete taxonomy of rich fields that could leverage a "System One" judgment layer, both within Twyne and more generally, covering what's deterministic versus what Jev adds, the interaction model, and practical concerns like latency.

Jev would need to run on a debounce (~400-650ms) rather than per-keystroke given network round-trip cost, though it's cheap and fast otherwise; Twyne's current shared budget of 12 calls/60s would need a dedicated lane for rich fields. I'm sketching pattern families: a "Recognize" field that parses free text into structured soft tokens (dotted underline, click to harden into explicit syntax) alongside deterministic hard tokens, and a "Grade inline" field that scores spans as you type, like flagging vague phrasing in real time.

Then there's "Resolve references" — text mentioning things in the project ("the river paragraph," "what I said about the ledger earlier") gets resolved via Choice into link chips or threads, essentially the no-@ version of mentions, which ties directly into Twyne's Threads feature. And "Route intent" — a single command field where free text gets classified into typed actions with args, shown as confirmable tokens before executing, like turning "make this shorter and less hedgy" into a structured rewrite command.

Next, "Constrain/validate" fields parse rules like word limits or forbidden topics into machine-checkable constraints that live-check against the draft inline, turning the field into a dashboard. Then "Consistency" checks flag cross-field contradictions (like a playful tone against a grieving audience), and "Complete/fill" ranks autocomplete suggestions contextually, as in resolving a vague citation reference to the right book.

Disambiguation handles cases like "Mercury" meaning planet versus element versus singer, surfacing low-confidence choices as a small fork in the field. Applied to Twyne, this means dossier fields get span-grading and constraint extraction, while comment composer and margin notes get reference resolution and intent detection — so a note like "TODO: check date" automatically routes itself into a task token.

For other fields: the find/search box could run natural language semantic search over the manuscript (combining semantic matching with hard filters like chapter or dialogue type), find/replace could handle conditional replacements by asking per-match whether a phrase refers to the intended meaning, and a research query field would parse into target types like claims, quotes, or statistics.

Other spots: selection "ask" fields route intent to the right instrument, rubric criterion editors check whether each criterion is actually falsifiable, personas get generated from trait descriptions, and bibliography paste fields could parse free citation text into structured entries.

For voice/dictation fields, the transcript needs tokens distinguishing commands ("new paragraph") from actual content, and character/place name fields in story bibles need consistency checking. The manuscript itself is the biggest rich field, and the highlighting pattern that overlays text without touching the DOM (ProseMirror's decorations) is exactly how in-line instruments should render.

The core design principle is two layers of tokens: hard tokens from syntax/code that are instant and certain, versus soft tokens from Jev that appear on pause and are probabilistic — shown visually as solid versus dotted, converting only on explicit click or Tab, never silently. Since Jev can't return precise character offsets, code needs to propose candidate spans itself.

I'm working out that Jev picks labels per span using batched Choice calls with a "none" option, debouncing requests and dropping stale answers by text hash. Probability should only surface where it changes behavior, and the real insight is that the parsed value becomes the API itself — fields emit structured output that downstream judges act on directly, generalizing the probe pattern to recognize structure within prose rather than asking separate typed questions. Cost-wise, this is cheap per check, but Twyne's shared rate limits mean rich fields need their own budget allocation.

I'm thinking a visual mockup would help here — showing an audience field with span grading, a constraints field turning into live checks, a find field converting natural language to tokens and results, a comment composer resolving implicit references, and a conditional replace example. I'll keep it compact since rich fields are inherently visual, and I'll also append a concise "Rich fields" section to the design doc for continuity, skipping any actual prototyping since I likely don't have API access to test against Jev.

## Rich fields: plain text that understands itself

Bramus's [`<rich-input>`](https://rich-input.netlify.app/) is a single-line input that recognises `keyword:value` tokens as you type. It highlights them in place with the CSS Custom Highlight API (no DOM changes), completes them from a `<datalist>`, and returns a parsed value (`getParsedQuery()`). The field stays plain text, yet produces structure.

Its tokens depend on syntax. System One makes the same idea work for prose with no syntax. That gives every field two layers:

- **Hard tokens:** recognised by code. Syntax, numbers, dates, quoted strings, `@names`, and exact matches against known entities. They are instant and certain, shown with a solid underline.
- **Soft tokens:** recognised by Jev when typing pauses. They are probabilistic, shown with a dotted underline, and Tab or a click turns one into a hard token. A soft token is never converted silently.

**Code proposes spans; Jev labels them.** Jev returns no character offsets. Code splits the field into candidate spans (clauses, noun phrases, quoted runs, capitalised runs, known names). One batched request then asks a Choice for each span over the field's label set plus `none`, or a Choice over project IDs when the span refers to something. This is the cookbook's pre-parsed value extraction pattern. Responses are dropped if the text has changed since the request (quick review already does this). The parsed value, not the prose, is what downstream judges receive. That generalises dossier probes: instead of asking a separate typed question, read the structure out of the answer the writer already gave.

| Field in Twyne | Hard tokens (code) | Soft tokens (Jev) | What the writer gets |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Audience / goal / tone | — | Score each span on brief-coach's levels (Vague → Sharp) | Brief coaching moves from the whole field to the actual words: "general readers" marked vague, "nurses who already know triage" marked sharp |
| Constraints | `under 1500 words`, quoted phrases | `avoid:"the lawsuit"`, `style:no jargon`, `pov:first person` | Each constraint becomes a rule checked live against the draft and shown inside the field (`1,812 / 1,500`) and in the Charter |
| Find | `in:ch3`, `kind:dialogue`, `"exact"` | Description → Choice over sentence IDs, plus a Noul for whether any match exists | "where I first mention the ledger" or "every place I hedge about the flood" become a search |
| Replace | the literal match list | One Noul per match ("here, does *the town* mean its people?") | Conditional replace: only the matches where it means what you meant |
| Comment composer | `@persona`, `#todo` | Reference resolution ("what I said about the ledger earlier" → `S012`); intent (note to self / question for a persona / task) | A comment that links its own evidence, draws a thread, and routes itself |
| Research query | years, quoted titles | Target kind (claim / quote / person / statistic / event / work) and the claim span it supports | The `research-targets` types filled from the query itself, shown before searching |
| Command bar / selection "ask" | `/rewrite`, `/move` | Intent and arguments ("shorter, less hedgy" → `rewrite(length: shorter, hedges: remove)`); the function-calling pattern | The parsed action is shown as tokens before Enter, so you see what will happen |
| Rubric criterion / Claim Check slot | — | Noul: "could a draft fail this?" | Criteria that rule nothing out are flagged as you type them |
| Bibliography paste | candidate authors, years, and titles found by regex | Which candidate fills which field | A messy citation becomes a structured entry |
| Cross-field | — | Noul: do tone and audience conflict? | Both conflicting spans are underlined and linked |

The manuscript is the largest rich field of all. "In the line" instruments should use the same pattern, rendered as ProseMirror decorations rather than marks, just as `<rich-input>` uses highlights rather than markup.

Cost and limits: Jev 1.13 charges $0.042 per million input tokens and allows 80 requests/s. A 300-token check costs about a thousandth of a cent, so the binding limit is Twyne's own judgement budget (12 calls/min shared across all features). Rich fields need their own budget lane, debounced to a pause of about 600 ms.

## Foundation fixes (prerequisites)

lines: Batch every independent question for the same state into one request (`system-one.ts` already supports this).
+## Rich fields: plain text that understands itself

+Bramus's [`<rich-input>`](https://rich-input.netlify.app/) is a single-line input that recognises `keyword:value` tokens as you type. It highlights them in place with the CSS Custom Highlight API (no DOM changes), completes them from a `<datalist>`, and returns a parsed value (`getParsedQuery()`). The field stays plain text, yet produces structure.
+Its tokens depend on syntax. System One makes the same idea work for prose with no syntax. That gives every field two layers:
+- **Hard tokens:** recognised by code. Syntax, numbers, dates, quoted strings, `@names`, and exact matches against known entities. They are instant and certain, shown with a solid underline.

+- **Soft tokens:** recognised by Jev when typing pauses. They are probabilistic, shown with a dotted underline, and Tab or a click turns one into a hard token. A soft token is never converted silently.

+**Code proposes spans; Jev labels them.** Jev returns no character offsets. Code splits the field into candidate spans (clauses, noun phrases, quoted runs, capitalised runs, known names). One batched request then asks a Choice for each span over the field's label set plus `none`, or a Choice over project IDs when the span refers to something. This is the cookbook's pre-parsed value extraction pattern. Responses are dropped if the text has changed since the request (quick review already does this). The parsed value, not the prose, is what downstream judges receive. That generalises dossier probes: instead of asking a separate typed question, read the structure out of the answer the writer already gave.
+| Field in Twyne | Hard tokens (code) | Soft tokens (Jev) | What the writer gets |

+| Audience / goal / tone | — | Score each span on brief-coach's levels (Vague → Sharp) | Brief coaching moves from the whole field to the actual words: "general readers" marked vague, "nurses who already know triage" marked sharp |

+| Constraints | `under 1500 words`, quoted phrases | `avoid:"the lawsuit"`, `style:no jargon`, `pov:first person` | Each constraint becomes a rule checked live against the draft and shown inside the field (`1,812 / 1,500`) and in the Charter |

+| Find | `in:ch3`, `kind:dialogue`, `"exact"` | Description → Choice over sentence IDs, plus a Noul for whether any match exists | "where I first mention the ledger" or "every place I hedge about the flood" become a search |
+| Replace | the literal match list | One Noul per match ("here, does *the town* mean its people?") | Conditional replace: only the matches where it means what you meant |

+| Comment composer | `@persona`, `#todo` | Reference resolution ("what I said about the ledger earlier" → `S012`); intent (note to self / question for a persona / task) | A comment that links its own evidence, draws a thread, and routes itself |

+| Research query | years, quoted titles | Target kind (claim / quote / person / statistic / event / work) and the claim span it supports | The `research-targets` types filled from the query itself, shown before searching |

+| Command bar / selection "ask" | `/rewrite`, `/move` | Intent and arguments ("shorter, less hedgy" → `rewrite(length: shorter, hedges: remove)`); the function-calling pattern | The parsed action is shown as tokens before Enter, so you see what will happen |
+| Rubric criterion / Claim Check slot | — | Noul: "could a draft fail this?" | Criteria that rule nothing out are flagged as you type them |
+| Bibliography paste | candidate authors, years, and titles found by regex | Which candidate fills which field | A messy citation becomes a structured entry |
+| Cross-field | — | Noul: do tone and audience conflict? | Both conflicting spans are underlined and linked |

+The manuscript is the largest rich field of all. "In the line" instruments should use the same pattern, rendered as ProseMirror decorations rather than marks, just as `<rich-input>` uses highlights rather than markup.

content.text:
Yes, `<rich-input>` is a good model for this. It's a plain-text field that recognizes `keyword:value` tokens as you type and returns structured data, while still looking like an ordinary input. Its limit is that it only spots tokens written in its syntax. Jev can spot the same kinds of thing in ordinary sentences, so any free-text field in Twyne could produce structured data without the writer learning a syntax.

I added a "Rich fields" section to `docs/writing-instruments.md` with the full table of fields. A few things the mockup doesn't show:

- **How it works:** Jev can't return character positions, so it can't find spans by itself. Code splits the field into candidate spans first (clauses, noun phrases, quoted text, names already in the project). One batched Jev request then labels each span or links it to a passage ID. This is TypeSafe's "pre-parsed value extraction" pattern. If the splitter misses a span, Jev can't select it, so most of the engineering goes into the splitter.
- **The big change:** downstream code receives the parsed value, not the prose. The constraints field shows this best. "Don't mention the lawsuit" becomes a rule that's checked against the draft continuously. Today it's a sentence a model has to remember to respect.
- **It extends work already in the code:**
  - The brief coach already grades each brief field as Vague, Partial or Sharp. Doing that per span is mostly a change in presentation.
  - The research target types already exist; the query field would just fill them in.
  - Margin notes that resolve "what I said about the ledger earlier" use the same sentence-ID lookup as Threads, so both features share that work.
- **Cost:** Jev is cheap enough to run on every pause. The real limit is Twyne's own rule of 12 Jev calls per minute, shared across every feature. Rich fields would need a separate allowance, triggered after about 600 ms without typing, and replies that arrive after the text has changed should be thrown away.

To start, I'd build either:
- **conditional replace:** the smallest, entirely in `find-replace-panel.tsx`, and easy to test; or
- **the constraints field:** more useful, because it turns the dossier into checks that actually run against the draft.

Should I build one of these, or go back to Phase 1 of the Sentence bench first?

content.thinking:
I realize the scoring is whole-draft rubric criteria, which is why the score can't update incrementally without rerunning everything on save events. The fix is to decompose scoring into per-section or per-paragraph criteria so feedback feels responsive rather than static.

Static features are already pure code, so they can update on every keystroke instantly, while Jev passage scores update on a debounce, and global scores can be marked stale and refreshed on a slower cadence. I also notice the voice consistency criterion could link directly to a concrete finding like I/we pronoun mixing, giving a clean mapping between findings and rubric criteria — and now I want to work out how that specific detection would actually run in code.

I'm sketching the pronoun detection logic: scan for first-person singular and plural pronouns outside quotes, exclude dialogue, then send ambiguous "we/us/our" instances to Jev with surrounding context to classify the stance (editorial we, inclusive we, group we, character speech, generic). Code then tallies the results into a finding like "31 I vs 4 editorial we," visualizes it as minimap ticks, and offers a rule-based fix to convert editorial-we sentences to first-person singular with proper verb agreement.

I'm also noting that this same pattern — code detects, Jev classifies ambiguous cases, code aggregates and offers batched fixes — applies to other consistency checks too, like narration tense per paragraph.

Beyond that, there's POV/interiority tracking in fiction to catch head-hopping, entity-alias clustering to confirm whether different names refer to the same person, drifting terminology for the same concept caught via embeddings plus Jev judgment, and style-sheet concerns like US/UK spelling and serial comma consistency.

I'm also thinking about an auto-generated style sheet (majority rule with flagged minorities) covering number formatting, dates, capitalization, and hyphenation — a classic copyeditor artifact that fits Twyne's exacting, editorial brand. Beyond that, there's register/formality tracked per paragraph, tracking who "you" addresses, and building an entity index ("bible") of characters, places, and concepts with code extracting candidate entities and Jev classifying their type, then mapping appearances into a timeline.

For relationships, I'd have code pair co-occurring entities per paragraph and Jev classify the relationship type and tension score, tracking how these shift across chapters into relationship arcs shown as a clickable graph linking back to establishing passages. For attributes and continuity, code would gather sentences mentioning a character while Jev selects the specific span answering a targeted question (like eye color), choosing among candidate spans or "none" rather than generating free text.

Comparing selected values across chapters would surface contradictions, and a similar structure could track knowledge state — who learns which secret by which chapter. A more novel test is voice distinctness: code attributes dialogue by speaker pattern, then Jev blind-attributes unattributed lines by choosing among characters, and the attribution accuracy per character becomes a concrete distinctness score — if Mara's lines keep getting assigned to Tom, their voices blur together. Nonfiction has analogous structures: claim graphs with evidence and counterarguments, source graphs, and concept introduction ordering, plus outline-level health checks at the structural level.

At structure level, each outline section could carry badges for word share versus importance, unresolved findings, and local score heat, building on the existing document outline and drag reorder — adding a section similarity matrix via embeddings to flag topics discussed far apart that should merge, plus Jev weighing in on section ordering. Promises and payoffs could become a live ledger tracking kept/pending/broken status, extending the existing "promises" lens. Other additions: pacing/tension curves per section, scene/sequel balance, dialogue-to-narration ratios computed in code, and an argument spine where Jev selects spans and code draws the thesis-to-support tree. At the collection level, I'm thinking about a series bible shared across folios.

Now for the "living application" layer — the score needs to function as a live instrument attributed directly to the text. Currently each criterion gets one score over the whole draft, rerun after save with a 30-second floor and 500-word minimum, with static features computed in code at review time. I want to split this into three cadences: instant code-based feedback (static features, ledger counts, style sheet), paragraph-pause feedback from Jev (local criterion scores, ledger classification), and periodic whole-document Jev scoring for criteria like thesis and structure, shown with staleness indicators. The composite score would combine weighted paragraph aggregation — using min-pooling so a weak paragraph pulls down the score — with global criteria, and changing weights shouldn't require rerunning anything.

For the delta display, when a paragraph's evidence score shifts, I want the UI to animate the change and attribute it to that specific paragraph, same for ledger fixes. But there's a calibration concern: paragraph-level scores may not aggregate cleanly into a whole-draft judgment, so I think the honest approach is to keep the whole-document score as the anchor, show paragraph scores as attribution rather than the score itself, and mark headline grades as estimated (≈) until the periodic pass confirms them — letting the grade move live but snap to confirmed readings. Then for the impact-ranked worklist, each finding would carry an estimated score impact computed from criterion weight, the gap between target and current, and scope share.

Sorting that list by impact plus effort gives a sense of what's actually important, and users could filter by criterion to see a heat map. Expanding a collapsed finding card should pull the manuscript into that lens — highlighting occurrences, dimming everything else, showing minimap ticks, scoping the panel to that finding, previewing fixes as ghost text, and shrinking or completing the card on acceptance. I'm also picturing a minimap/document spine running alongside the page, showing heat by criterion, ledger ticks, and character presence, acting as the document-level view with clickable jumps. And then lenses — toggles like Stance, Tense, Characters — that re-render the manuscript accordingly.

Now I'm sketching the card schema itself: level (word through collection), scope as anchored spans, a live metric with trend, which rubric criterion it feeds, estimated impact, available actions (fix, review, set rule, open lens, dismiss), provenance (rule/Jev/LLM), and state (open/improving/resolved/deliberate). The "deliberate" state feels important since writers often vary style on purpose — marking something deliberate should silence the nagging and get folded into the charter of rules guiding future Jev questions. I'm also weighing the cost implications of running per-paragraph Jev scoring on every pause, given token costs for scoring against ten criteria per paragraph.

The real cost looks negligible per request, but the actual constraint is rate limits, so I need a scheduler that batches dirty paragraphs rather than firing a call per edit. ## Levels: the whole piece, not just the sentence

Sentence work is one level of six. Help needs to reach every level, and the most useful findings often span the whole document. Examples: an essay that slides between "I" and an editorial "we", a character called Hollins in chapter 2 and Hollis in chapter 9, a section that disappears from the argument.

| Level | Examples of what to notice | Who finds it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Word | Repeated words, near-synonyms, unlikely words | Code, fill-mask model |
| Sentence | Rewording, placement, rhythm | Sentence bench (above) |
| Paragraph | Missing support, cohesion, how much it carries | Jev passage scores, embeddings |
| Section / scene | Balance, order, tension, point of view | Jev, outline, embeddings |
| Piece | Stance, tense, naming, terminology, promises, arcs, the score | Ledgers (below) |
| Collection | Story bible, repeated anecdotes, voice over time | Cross-folio index |

### Consistency ledgers

A ledger tracks one property across the whole document. It always has the same shape:

1. **Code finds every occurrence**, instantly and offline: pronouns outside quotation marks, verb tenses (a local POS tagger such as `compromise` is worth evaluating), capitalised names, spelling variants by edit distance, number and date formats.
2. **Jev classifies only the ambiguous ones**, many per batched request (`passage-triage.ts` already chunks batches against the 64-question cap).
3. **Code totals them and keeps the count live** as the writer edits.
4. **Code offers a fix with a preview**, one occurrence at a time or all at once, plus a **Deliberate** option. Deliberate records the choice as a Charter rule, so the ledger stops nagging and future drift is flagged straight away.

**Stance (I / we) is the clearest case.** A regex can count "we", but it can't tell what the "we" means. For each "we/us/our" outside dialogue, Jev answers one Choice with the sentence before it as context:

- the author alone (editorial or royal we)
- the author and the reader ("as we'll see")
- a group the author belongs to (family, team, town)
- a character speaking
- people in general

Only an editorial "we" mixed with a mostly-"I" piece is a problem. Inclusive and group "we" are normal, and a regex alone would flag them. The fix is mostly deterministic: we→I, us→me, our→my, ourselves→myself, with verb agreement (we are→I am, we were→I was). Harper then checks the result. Each fix moves the count and the Voice criterion.

Other ledgers built the same way:

- **Narrating tense:** one Jev Choice per paragraph (past / present / deliberate shift such as a flashback / unintended mix), ignoring dialogue.
- **Point of view per scene:** whose thoughts we have access to, a Choice over the cast; flags switching heads mid-scene.
- **Naming:** Hollins and Hollis are caught by code alone. Whether *Dr Okafor*, *Ada* and *the doctor* are the same person is a Jev Noul for each candidate pair.
- **Terminology:** "participants", "subjects" and "respondents" drifting for one concept is found by embeddings and confirmed by Jev. A term used before it is defined is caught by code once the definition has been located.
- **Style sheet:** US or UK spelling, serial comma, *ten* or *10*, date formats, hyphenation. Pure code, majority rule, with the exceptions flagged. This is a copyeditor's style sheet the writer gets for free, and it suits Twyne.
- **Who "you" is:** the reader, or anyone in general.
- **Register:** one Score per paragraph, plotted as a curve.

### Characters and entities

- **Index:** code proposes candidates (capitalised runs not at the start of a sentence, repeated "the X" phrases); Jev confirms the type (person / place / organisation / object / idea / none).
- **Presence grid:** entities × sections, computed by code. It shows a character missing for eight chapters, or a place that turns up only once.
- **Relationship web:** for each pair that appears in the same paragraph, a Jev Choice over relationship types and a Score for tension, per chapter. That gives relationship *arcs*. Each edge links to the spans that establish it.
- **Continuity:** for each attribute (eyes, age, coat), Jev picks which candidate span states it, or none. Code compares the values across chapters and turns contradictions into threads.
- **Do the voices differ? (blind attribution):** remove the speaker tags and ask Jev who said each line, as a Choice over the cast. If Mara's lines are attributed to Tom 60% of the time, they sound alike. Accuracy per character becomes a distinctness score.
- **Nonfiction:** the same machinery makes a claim web (claim → support → objection) and a concept map (where each concept is introduced, used, and dropped).

### Structure

- **Outline health:** each heading in the existing outline (`document-outline.ts`) gets badges: its share of the words, its open findings, and a score heat for the selected criterion. Dragging sections to reorder them (`section-reorder.ts`) gets suggestions: an embedding similarity matrix shows sections that belong together, and a Jev Choice suggests which section should come before a given one.
- **Promises and payoffs:** the "promises" lens becomes a ledger with a status for each promise: kept / open / dropped. One Noul asks whether the ending answers the question the opening raises.
- **Pacing:** dialogue-to-narration ratio and section length (code), tension (a Jev Score per paragraph), drawn as curves along the outline.

## The living score

Today the rubric asks one Jev Score per criterion of the whole draft (`rubric-grade.ts` `buildRubricQuestions`). It runs after a save, at most once per 30 s, and only for drafts over 500 words. The score therefore cannot say *where* it comes from or move while you edit. `scoreStaticFeatures` is pure code that could run on every keystroke, but it is only called at review time.

**Three cadences:**

| Cadence | What updates | Engine |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Instant | Static features, ledger counts, style sheet, presence grid | Code |
| When a paragraph settles | That paragraph's scores for local criteria (evidence, integrity, pacing, voice); classification of new ledger occurrences | Jev, batched across dirty paragraphs |
| Periodically | Whole-piece criteria (thesis, target fit, structure, promises) | Jev, labelled "read 3 min ago" and marked stale once enough has changed |

**Attribution and honesty.** Paragraph scores show *where the grade comes from*: a heat map per criterion. Code combines them using the composite-scoring pattern (weighted, with a penalty for the weakest paragraph, because readers notice the worst one). The headline grade moves with these estimates, marked ≈, and settles on the confirmed whole-piece reading when it arrives. Paragraph scores averaged together have not been shown to agree with whole-draft judgements; validate that on real drafts before trusting the estimate.

**What matters most.** Every finding, at every level, carries an estimated impact: criterion weight × the distance to the next score level × how much of the piece it covers. It also carries an effort: the number of edits needed. Findings are sorted by impact, so the writer can see what is worth fixing.

**Cards at every level** share one shape:

- `level`: word / sentence / paragraph / section / piece / collection
- `scope`: anchored spans, from 1 up to dozens
- `metric`: a live count or score, with its trend
- `criterion`: which rubric criterion it feeds, used for impact
- `actions`: fix one / review all / make it a rule / open lens / dismiss with reason
- `provenance`: rule, Jev, or text model
- `state`: open / improving / resolved / deliberate

Collapsed, a card is one line with a live number. Expanded, it takes over the document: the manuscript switches to that card's **lens** (matches highlighted, everything else dimmed), and a **document spine** beside the page shows the whole piece as a strip with ticks where the finding occurs. Each fix previews as ghost text. Accepting it updates the count, the minimap tick, the criterion bar, and the headline grade together.

The document spine is the permanent view of the whole piece: sections, heat for the selected criterion, ticks for the open lens, character presence. Clicking any point jumps to that spot.

+- **Nonfiction:** the same machinery makes a claim web (claim → support → objection) and a concept map (where each concept is introduced, used, and dropped).
+### Structure

+- **Outline health:** each heading in the existing outline (`document-outline.ts`) gets badges: its share of the words, its open findings, and a score heat for the selected criterion. Dragging sections to reorder them (`section-reorder.ts`) gets suggestions: an embedding similarity matrix shows sections that belong together, and a Jev Choice suggests which section should come before a given one.
+- **Promises and payoffs:** the "promises" lens becomes a ledger with a status for each promise: kept / open / dropped. One Noul asks whether the ending answers the question the opening raises.
+- **Pacing:** dialogue-to-narration ratio and section length (code), tension (a Jev Score per paragraph), drawn as curves along the outline.
+## The living score

+Today the rubric asks one Jev Score per criterion of the whole draft (`rubric-grade.ts` `buildRubricQuestions`). It runs after a save, at most once per 30 s, and only for drafts over 500 words. The score therefore cannot say *where* it comes from or move while you edit. `scoreStaticFeatures` is pure code that could run on every keystroke, but it is only called at review time.
+**Three cadences:**
+| Cadence | What updates | Engine |
+| Instant | Static features, ledger counts, style sheet, presence grid | Code |
+| When a paragraph settles | That paragraph's scores for local criteria (evidence, integrity, pacing, voice); classification of new ledger occurrences | Jev, batched across dirty paragraphs |
+| Periodically | Whole-piece criteria (thesis, target fit, structure, promises) | Jev, labelled "read 3 min ago" and marked stale once enough has changed |

+**Attribution and honesty.** Paragraph scores show *where the grade comes from*: a heat map per criterion. Code combines them using the composite-scoring pattern (weighted, with a penalty for the weakest paragraph, because readers notice the worst one). The headline grade moves with these estimates, marked ≈, and settles on the confirmed whole-piece reading when it arrives. Paragraph scores averaged together have not been shown to agree with whole-draft judgements; validate that on real drafts before trusting the estimate.

+**What matters most.** Every finding, at every level, carries an estimated impact: criterion weight × the distance to the next score level × how much of the piece it covers. It also carries an effort: the number of edits needed. Findings are sorted by impact, so the writer can see what is worth fixing.
+**Cards at every level** share one shape:
+- `level`: word / sentence / paragraph / section / piece / collection
+- `scope`: anchored spans, from 1 up to dozens
+- `metric`: a live count or score, with its trend
+- `criterion`: which rubric criterion it feeds, used for impact
+- `actions`: fix one / review all / make it a rule / open lens / dismiss with reason
+- `provenance`: rule, Jev, or text model
+- `state`: open / improving / resolved / deliberate

+Collapsed, a card is one line with a live number. Expanded, it takes over the document: the manuscript switches to that card's **lens** (matches highlighted, everything else dimmed), and a **document spine** beside the page shows the whole piece as a strip with ticks where the finding occurs. Each fix previews as ghost text. Accepting it updates the count, the minimap tick, the criterion bar, and the headline grade together.
+The document spine is the permanent view of the whole piece: sections, heat for the selected criterion, ticks for the open lens, character presence. Clicking any point jumps to that spot.
## Rich fields: plain text that understands itself

Bramus's [`<rich-input>`](https://rich-input.netlify.app/) is a single-line input that recognises `keyword:value` tokens as you type. It highlights them in place with the CSS Custom Highlight API (no DOM changes), completes them from a `<datalist>`, and returns a parsed value (`getParsedQuery()`). The field stays plain text, yet produces structure.

input.content:
Lens Click a card · fix · watch it move

I. The warning

I was nine the spring the river came up through Hollins. We kids were sent to the church hall, where Mara Okafor counted us at the door. I remember her pencil more than the water.

We would argue that the archive was never neutral. I spent two winters in it, and the warnings are filed in the order they were answered, not the order they were sent.

II. The town

As we'll see, the order matters. Hollins had two sirens and one man who knew how to work both. When he drove north to check the levee, the south siren stayed quiet.

Every family lost something that spring. The ones on the north bank lost the most, and theirs are the accounts the archive kept.

III. The ledger

Mara kept the church ledger: names, times, what was carried in. Here we must admit the record is thin, but it is honest about being thin.

Our view is that the ledger, not the archive, holds the town's memory. I have read it more times than I can count, and on every page Hollis reads like a smaller town than the one I grew up in.

6.3

Lens Click a card · fix · watch it move

I. The warning

I was nine the spring the river came up through Hollins. We kids were sent to the church hall, where Mara Okafor counted us at the door. I remember her pencil more than the water.

We would argue that the archive was never neutral. I spent two winters in it, and the warnings are filed in the order they were answered, not the order they were sent.

II. The town

As we'll see, the order matters. Hollins had two sirens and one man who knew how to work both. When he drove north to check the levee, the south siren stayed quiet.

Every family lost something that spring. The ones on the north bank lost the most, and theirs are the accounts the archive kept.

III. The ledger

Mara kept the church ledger: names, times, what was carried in. Here we must admit the record is thin, but it is honest about being thin.

Our view is that the ledger, not the archive, holds the town's memory. I have read it more times than I can count, and on every page Hollis reads like a smaller town than the one I grew up in.
